method: Rebuild from primary text. Gov. Code §12952 was fetched in full from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and read subdivision by subdivision. CourtListener was searched for decisions construing the section. Assertions describe the REBUILT body; the previous body's errors are under priorDefects.
queries: "Government Code section 12952" fair chance conviction history conditional offer

assertions.text: the section applies to an employer with five or more employees
assertions.note: §12952(a): 'it is an unlawful employment practice for an employer with five or more employees'. The previous body stated the whole procedure unconditionally.

assertions.text: no question seeking conviction history may appear on an application, and no inquiry into or consideration of conviction history may occur, until after a conditional offer

arrests not followed by conviction, diversion referrals or participation, and convictions sealed, dismissed, expunged, statutorily eradicated, pardoned or subject to a certificate of rehabilitation may not be considered, distributed or disseminated
assertions.note: §12952(a)(3)(A)-(C). Absent from the previous body entirely, and it is the part most likely to be violated by a background-check vendor's raw report.

assertions.text: an employer intending to deny solely or in part because of conviction history must make an individualized assessment of whether the conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job that justify denying the position
assertions.note: §12952(c)(1)(A), and quoted in those words by the Court of Appeal in Shikha v. Lyft. The previous body listed the three factors but never stated the test they feed, so an assessment could recite the factors and reach no finding.

assertions.text: the assessment must consider the nature and gravity of the offense or conduct, the time that has passed since the offense or conduct and completion of the sentence, and the nature of the job held or sought
the employer may, but is not required to, commit the results of the individualized assessment to writing
assertions.note: §12952(c)(1)(B), verbatim. The previous body instructed the reader to 'perform a written individualized assessment', which states a duty the section does not impose. This is the one error in the previous body that ran against the employer rather than the applicant.

assertions.text: a preliminary decision to disqualify must be notified in writing and must contain the disqualifying convictions, a copy of the conviction history report if any, and an explanation of the right to respond with the deadline
assertions.note: §12952(c)(2)(A)-(C). The notification may but need not explain the employer's reasoning. The previous body required 'a preliminary notice with a copy of the report' and omitted both the 'if any' and the explanation of the right to respond.

assertions.text: the applicant has at least five business days to respond, and five additional business days if within that period the applicant notifies the employer in writing that the applicant disputes the accuracy of the report and is taking specific steps to obtain supporting evidence
assertions.note: §12952(c)(3). The previous body gave 'an additional five (5) days', dropping 'business', and omitted both conditions on the extension — the written notification and the taking of specific steps. The extension is not automatic on a bare dispute.

assertions.text: a final decision to deny must be notified in writing and must state the denial, any existing procedure the employer has to challenge it or request reconsideration, and the right to file a complaint with the department
assertions.note: §12952(c)(5)(A)-(C). The previous body said the final decision carries 'the right to appeal'. There is no statutory right of appeal; there is notice of whatever internal procedure the employer happens to have, and the right to complain to the Civil Rights Department. An employer with no internal procedure owes no appeal and the previous body implied otherwise.

assertions.text: the section does not apply to positions where a state or local agency is required by law to conduct a conviction history check, to criminal justice agencies, to Farm Labor Contractor positions, or where any state, federal or local law requires a criminal background check or restricts employment based on criminal history

priorDefects: contradicted: 'perform a written individualized assessment' — §12952(c)(1)(B) says the employer may but is not required to put it in writing.

contradicted: 'a final written decision with the right to appeal' — §12952(c)(5) requires notice of any existing employer procedure and of the right to file a complaint with the department, not a right of appeal.
omitted: 'business' from the second five-day period (§12952(c)(3)).
omitted: the two conditions on the five-day extension — written notice of the dispute and that the applicant is taking specific steps to obtain evidence (§12952(c)(3)).
omitted: the statutory test — direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job (§12952(c)(1)(A)).
omitted: §12952(a)(3), the categories of record that may not be considered at all.
unsupported: 'Job advertisements must not state that people with criminal histories will not be considered.' No such prohibition appears anywhere in §12952. See gaps.
gaps: The advertisement prohibition asserted by the previous body is not in §12952. It is carried into the rebuilt body only as an explicitly flagged unverified item, because it may rest on the Civil Rights Department's regulations at 2 CCR §11017.1 or on a local ordinance. It could not be confirmed: the official publisher of the California Code of Regulations, govt.westlaw.com, returns HTTP 403 at this environment's egress proxy, so the regulation text was never opened. It is recorded as unverified rather than deleted or asserted.

The 2023 Civil Rights Department regulations also set when the five-day response period starts running where receipt cannot be confirmed. That timing rule is in the regulations, not in §12952, and for the same reason could not be read from its publisher. The clause therefore states the periods without the receipt-timing trigger, and says so.

No decision construing §12952 was found on CourtListener. Shikha v. Lyft quotes the individualized-assessment test in passing while discussing criminal-history policy generally; it does not construe any element. The section appears to be essentially unconstrued in the published case law, which means the statutory text is doing all the work and any ambiguity in it remains open.

sources.title: California Legislative Counsel (leginfo) — Cal. Gov. Code §12952
CourtListener — Shikha v. Lyft, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App., May 17, 2024)

judicialQuotations.case: Shikha v. Lyft, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2024)
judicialQuotations.quote: Under Government Code section 12952, the Fair Chance Act, employers generally may not ask about a job candidate's criminal history before making a conditional job offer. (Gov. Code, § 12952, subd. (a)(1),(2).)

judicialQuotations.case: Shikha v. Lyft, Inc. (Cal. Ct. App. 2024)
judicialQuotations.quote: employer must "make an individualized assessment of whether the applicant's conviction history has a direct and adverse relationship with the specific duties of the job that justify denying the applicant the position." (Gov. Code, § 12952, subd. (c)(1)(A).)

singleOpinionCaveat: Shikha v. Lyft is not a construction of §12952. Both quotations are the court restating the statute while surveying criminal-history restrictions in an unrelated context. They corroborate that the text on leginfo is the operative text and nothing more. The rebuild rests on the statute.
